books.section: Topic 8.7 America as a World Power
Topic 8.2 The Cold War from 1945 to 1980
Unit 8: The Postwar Period and Cold War (1945-1980)

primary_sources: Harry S. Truman, address to Congress, March 12, 1947 (paraphrased)
John Foster Dulles, speech to the Council on Foreign Relations, January 12, 1954 (paraphrased)
Dwight D. Eisenhower, Farewell Address, January 17, 1961 (paraphrased)

source: original; documents are paraphrases of public sources (see each document's sourcing note); the photograph is a public-domain U.S. Marine Corps photograph viewed before writing

stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the United States acted as a world power through the policy of containment from 1947 to 1961.

documents.title: Aid to Greece and Turkey
documents.source: Paraphrase of President Harry S. Truman's address to Congress, March 12, 1947.
documents.sourcing: Truman is asking Congress for money and for a public commitment, so he frames aid as a defense of freedom, not only as help to two countries.
documents.text: Paraphrase of President Harry S. Truman's address to Congress, March 12, 1947. Truman asked Congress for 400 million dollars in aid to Greece and Turkey. He said the United States must support free peoples who were resisting subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures. He warned that if Greece fell, confusion and disorder might spread through the whole Middle East.

documents.title: Massive retaliation
documents.source: Paraphrase of Secretary of State John Foster Dulles's speech to the Council on Foreign Relations, January 12, 1954.
documents.sourcing: Dulles is explaining a new administration's policy to a foreign-policy audience, so he stresses deterrence and low cost, not the risks of the threat.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Secretary of State John Foster Dulles's speech, January 12, 1954. Dulles said the United States would depend more on nuclear weapons and air power than on large ground armies. If a Communist power attacked the free world, the United States would retaliate instantly, with means and places of its own choosing. The threat of such massive retaliation would deter aggression at far lower cost.

documents.title: A government falls in Guatemala
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Central Intelligence Agency's declassified account of the 1954 operation in Guatemala.
documents.sourcing: The account comes from the agency that ran the operation, so it describes the coup as a success and says little about the Guatemalans who lost their government.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Central Intelligence Agency's account of the 1954 operation in Guatemala. President Jacobo Arbenz had taken unused land from the United Fruit Company for redistribution to peasants. The agency trained and armed an opposition force, which drove Arbenz from office in June 1954 and installed a military government in his place.

documents.title: Winter war in Korea
documents.source: Photograph: U.S. Marine Corps, Korean War, winter 1950-1951. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
documents.sourcing: A U.S. Marine Corps photograph of American troops in the winter fighting, showing the war as the soldiers themselves endured it.
documents.text: The photograph shows United States Marines resting in deep snow beside a jeep during the Korean War. The men wear heavy winter clothing covered in snow, and several sit or lie exhausted along a snowy roadside.

documents.title: Eisenhower on Suez
documents.source: Paraphrase of President Dwight D. Eisenhower's radio and television address, October 31, 1956.
documents.sourcing: Eisenhower is speaking to the American public during an election week, so he presents the United States as a peacemaker standing apart from its own allies.
documents.text: Paraphrase of President Dwight D. Eisenhower's address, October 31, 1956. Eisenhower said the United States would not join Britain, France, and Israel in their attack on Egypt. He said there could be no peace without law, and he called on the United Nations to arrange a cease-fire and a withdrawal of the invading forces.

documents.title: A satellite crosses the sky
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Soviet announcement of the Sputnik launch, October 4, 1957, as reported in the American press.
documents.sourcing: The announcement is Soviet, so it celebrates the achievement; the American press reports add the alarm the launch caused in the United States.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Soviet announcement of the Sputnik launch, October 4, 1957. The Soviet Union announced that it had placed the first artificial satellite into orbit around the Earth. The satellite circled the planet, sending out a radio signal that listeners in many countries could hear. American newspapers reported the news with alarm, warning that the rockets that carried Sputnik could also carry weapons across oceans.

documents.title: A farewell warning
documents.source: Paraphrase of President Dwight D. Eisenhower's Farewell Address, January 17, 1961.
documents.sourcing: Eisenhower speaks as a departing president and a former general, so his warning about the military carries the weight of a man who built the forces he criticizes.
documents.text: Paraphrase of President Dwight D. Eisenhower's Farewell Address, January 17, 1961. Eisenhower warned Americans about the growth of a military-industrial complex, the close ties among the armed forces, the arms industry, and government. He said the United States needed a strong military, but he warned that this combination of interests could gain influence over public policy and endanger liberty.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the United States acted as a world power through containment from 1947 to 1961, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of American action does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the wartime alliance with the Soviet Union giving way to rivalry, or the United States emerging from World War II as the world's strongest economy.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant content from at least three documents, such as the Truman Doctrine, massive retaliation, and the Guatemala coup.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting or naming documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including the Korean War photograph and the farewell warning.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example outside the documents, such as the Marshall Plan, NATO, the Berlin Airlift, or the U-2 incident of 1960.
rubric.notEarned: Naming an outside example with no specific detail, or repeating a document's content, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation for at least two documents, such as Dulles speaking to a foreign-policy audience or the CIA describing its own operation.
rubric.notEarned: Restating a document's sourcing note without explaining why it matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the thesis by showing that containment made the United States a world power and also limited it, or weighing open war against covert action and nuclear threats.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: From 1947 to 1961 the United States acted as a world power to a great extent through containment, building alliances, sending aid, fighting a limited war, and threatening nuclear retaliation, but its power had limits, since it relied on secret action and threats rather than open control, and it could not stop every Communist advance.
Context: The United States came out of World War II as the world's strongest economy, while its wartime alliance with the Soviet Union broke down into rivalry over Eastern Europe and the future of Germany.
Evidence: Documents 1 and 2 show containment stated as policy, first as aid to free peoples and then as massive retaliation. Document 3 shows covert action in Guatemala, and Document 4 shows the open war in Korea, where American troops fought in bitter winter conditions. Document 5 shows the United States acting against its own allies at Suez, and Document 6 shows the Soviet challenge in space. Document 7 shows Eisenhower warning that the military power built for containment could itself endanger liberty.
Outside evidence: The Marshall Plan sent about 13 billion dollars to Western Europe, NATO bound the United States to Europe's defense in 1949, and the U-2 incident of 1960 exposed American spying over the Soviet Union.
Complexity: Containment made the United States a world power, but it also boxed the country in: open war in Korea ended in stalemate, covert coups bred resentment, and the nuclear threat that deterred war also left the country living under the fear of it.
